seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Dear Pound: In the first place many thanks for the numbered copy of your book Lustra which gave me great pleasure. I am sure you must be glad to have written verses so joyful and beautiful. I at least am very glad to have them near my hand as a relief from my own soporiferous writing. I hope to be able to send you this year in exchange a copy of my novel .

I sent yesterday the typescript of Exiles . If it is still under consideration in Chicago perhaps a postcard from you, alluding to the recent recognition of my writing, might act as a stimulant. If not by all means let it appear in the review Seven Arts
. I hope then to publish it in 1917. As regards Mr Knoblauch Knoblock
I think it is wise to wait until we hear what he says.

I have written to all the persons whose names and addresses you gave me and expressed to all my grateful thanks. As for yourself it is useless even to try to thank you. I know and feel however that I owe everything to your generous friendship and I hope that the energy which you say you will now devote to promoting your own interests will bring you every good fortune.

I received a letter this morning dated 11 August from Mr Quinn of New York enclosing a cheque for £10. His secretary it seems forgot to send the money till now. I have answered him too and I can now see my way ahead for a certain time during which, I hope, a change of fortune will set in for my books so that I may cease to be a burden to so many people.

Miss Weaver writes that she has had a letter from Mr Huebsch (25 August) asking her to see my agent and to beg him to give the matter of my book his immediate attention and to cable to him (Mr Huebsch) if the terms of the contract suited so that the book might appear in the autumn list. Miss Weaver went at once to Mr Pinker and it seems that the cablegram has been sent. Unfortunately Mr Huebsch had not at that date received from Mr Marshall who is in Quebec the corrected version of the text. Miss Weaver, to save time, corrected the text herself and sent it off and she sent me also by express the text so that I might correct it also and send it separately. Mr Huebsch however has written to Mr Marshall. Mr Quinn said that a Mr Kreymborg was reading the book and that perhaps it would be published by a Mr Alfred Knof Knopf
. God grant it be not published by too many persons at the same time.

I am sorry to say that, except the play, I have nothing else ready for Seven Arts but perhaps that would run to three numbers. I have a few pieces of verse by me. All the rest of my MSS is the bewildering mass of papers for Ulysses which I carry in a very large envelope that I possess for the last twelve years.
I am glad to see that you are as usual in good health and so am I.
With the kindest regards and an infinity of thanks

postscript.p:
P.S. I fear I may have misdirected the play. If so you could ask at the P.O. Perhaps in my hurry I sent it to: 5 Holland Place, instead of 5 Holland Place Chambers.
Bestia !

div.note: Postmark: The postmark is difficult to read, but the context of the letter points to September over October. A letter to John Quinn late Aug–early Sept 1916 is probably the letter mentioned here by JJ, and that letter mentions the Civil List award which happened in August.

Pound had sent JJ one of 200 numbered copies of his volume of poems, Lustra, privately printed in September 1916 for Elkin Mathews of London and available for sale to those specially requesting this unabridged edition. An abridged edition of Lustra was published by Mathews in October 1916 in the normal way. After the prosecution of D.H. Lawrence’s The Rainbow in England in 1915, Mathews and his printer had feared that certain frank poems in Lustra would lay the book open to legal proceedings. Issuance of private and public editions was the solution.

JJ’s novel A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man was published as a book in the United States by B.W. Huebsch of New York in December 1916, and in England by the Egoist Ltd. of London in February 1917.

JJ’s London literary agent J.B. Pinker had for months been trying to get JJ’s play Exiles accepted for publication in the Chicago review, Drama. Pinker learned of Drama’s rejection of the play in early November 1916 (John Firth, “James Pinker to James Joyce, 1915-1920,” Studies in Bibliography 21 [1968]: 218).

Pound thought the New York little magazine Seven Arts might be interested in printing Exiles (Pound/Joyce 83). Edited by James Oppenheim, Waldo Frank, and Van Wyck Brooks, Seven Arts was dedicated to what Brooks called “America’s Coming of Age,” and ran from November 1916 to October 1917. It took a strong anti-war stance and boasted among its contributors Sherwood Anderson, Theodore Dreiser, Robert Frost, Kahlil Gibran, D.H. Lawrence, and Amy Lowell, but never James Joyce. Seven Arts merged with The Dial in 1917 (Pound/Joyce 83 n. 5).

Edward Knoblock, born Knoblauch (1874-1945), American-born British playwright and novelist, best known for his play Kismet (1911). Pound met with him in early September 1916 and tried to persuade him to read JJ’s Exiles in the hope that he would adapt the play for the stage. In his letter of 6 September 1916, Pound asked JJ for “an authorization for a stage version if Knoblauch chooses to take it up” (Pound/Joyce 84), but JJ here replies that they should wait until Knoblock expresses serious interest. JJ’s caution was sensible. On 13 November 1916, Pound wrote, “Knoblock seems to have vanished” (Pound/Joyce 84). He did not adapt or stage Exiles.

Hoping to obtain further official financial assistance for JJ, Pound persuaded his acquaintance, American-born, London-based Lady Cunard, born Maud Alice Burke (1872-1948), to lend JJ’s books to the translator and editor Edward Marsh (1872-1953), who at the time was assistant private secretary to British Prime Minister H.H. Asquith (1852-1928). With letters of support from Yeats and the Irish novelist George Moore (1852-1933), JJ was awarded a grant of £100 from the British Civil List (Ellmann, JJ 405-06). At Pound’s urging, JJ wrote letters of thanks to Marsh and Yeats (LI 94-95).

After months of labor on behalf of Wyndham Lewis and other artists, as well as JJ, Pound hoped, as he wrote JJ in early September 1916, to “devote the next six months entirely to my own interests. (Which will do them no good whatever.)” (Pound/Joyce 82).

The New York lawyer and patron of the arts, John Quinn (1870-1924), decided to “stake” JJ to £10 when Pound declined a similar amount in favor of JJ. Quinn, though harried by many requests for financial assistance, took “pleasure” in helping JJ because, he told him, “I am interested in your work” (Pound/Joyce 75).

Harriet Shaw Weaver and JJ’s London literary agent J.B. Pinker were corresponding with B.W. Huebsch of New York about an American edition of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, which Huebsch soon accepted for publication and issued in December 1916. Weaver had written JJ about progress with Huebsch on 7 September 1916, and JJ replied to her on 16 September (LI 95-96). Huebsch’s letter to Weaver of 25 August 1916 is found at LI 93-94.

With characteristic generosity, Pound had urged the New York publisher John Marshall in March 1916 to publish JJ’s A Portrait in place of Pound’s own projected essay collection, “This Generation” (Pound/Joyce 5, 75). Marshall sent JJ an advance of £10, but soon left for Canada with his ailing wife and published neither JJ’s novel nor Pound’s collection. Pound wrote JJ on 22 July 1916 that Marshall had “given up his publishing ghost …. [He] seems blameless – wife collapsed with consumption & he with emotion” (Pound/Joyce 78). Pound took a less generous view of the disappearance of “This Generation” when he wrote the Little Review editors in July 1918 that there should be a “Lynch-law for manuscript thieves”; he included among his “vendettas” an “ex-New York publisher named Marshall (spurious verschwindet [vanishes]) [who] disappeared with mss. of a long book” (Pound/The Little Review: The Letters of Ezra Pound to Margaret Anderson: The Little Review Correspondence, ed. Thomas L. Scott and Melvin J. Friedman [New York: New Directions, 1988], 244-45). Pound never recovered the manuscript of “This Generation,” but a similar collection of Pound’s essays, Pavannes and Divisions, was published by Alfred A. Knopf of New York in June 1918.

The American author and editor Alfred Kreymborg (1883-1966) published a collection of verse, Mushrooms: A Book of Free Forms, with John Marshall of New York in 1916. With Man Ray, Kreymborg produced The Glebe, a New York little magazine that printed Des Imagistes: An Anthology, edited by Pound, in February 1914. Kreymborg also published poems by Pound in his magazine Others as well as in his collection, Others: An Anthology of the New Verse, issued by Alfred A. Knopf of New York in 1916. Kreymborg may have been reading A Portrait as a way of assisting either Knopf or John Marshall, both candidates for publishing JJ’s novel at the time (see above). Alfred A. Knopf (1892-1984) published many modern authors, but not Joyce.

It., lit. “beast.” Used here as an abbreviated form of the expletive, “Dio bestia,” “God is a beast.” This expression is similar to “dio boia,” the executioner god that Stephen Dedalus holds responsible in the “Scylla and Charybdis” episode of Ulysses for the calamities of life – a creator who “wrote the folio of this world and wrote it badly … the lord of things as they are whom the most Roman of catholics call dio boia, hangman god” (U 9.1047-49).
